estimand: θ = (μ₂ − μ₁)/μ₁ = μ₂/μ₁ − 1, the population relative effect of arm 2 versus arm 1, where μ_j = E[X_j] is the per-unit mean of the metric in arm j (for a ratio metric, μ_j is replaced by r_j = E[N_j]/E[D_j], a ratio of expectations, NOT E[N/D]). Reported as a two-sided 100(1−α)% confidence set for θ at the per-comparison (post-correction) level α, together with a point estimate θ̂ = m̂₂/m̂₁ − 1 and a p-value for H₀: θ = 0. Note that H₀: θ = 0 and H₀: μ₂ − μ₁ = 0 are the SAME hypothesis whenever μ₁ ≠ 0; any pair of methods that assigns them different p-values is internally incoherent, and that observation turns out to settle most of the question below.

assumptions.assumption: The two arm means m̂₁, m̂₂ are (jointly) asymptotically normal: m̂_j ~ N(μ_j, V_j), V_j = σ_j²/n_j.
assumptions.why_needed: Every interval here (delta, log, Fieller) is a normal-theory construction. Fieller is EXACT under exact bivariate normality of (m̂₁, m̂₂); the others are first-order.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: Heavy-tailed revenue with skewness γ needs roughly n > 25γ² (Cochran's rule) for one-sided error rates to be accurate at α=0.05; below that the one-sided errors are asymmetric and NO choice of variance formula fixes it — the CLT error dominates the ratio correction entirely. The engine cannot even diagnose this from n, Σx, Σx²: it would need Σx³. Recommend storing Σx³ (and Σx⁴) purely as a diagnostic.

assumptions.assumption: Independence of the two arms: Cov(m̂₁, m̂₂) = 0.
assumptions.why_needed: It kills the cross term in the delta expansion exactly, which is the crux of the question asked.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: In paired mode the cross term is real and first-order: Var(θ̂) ≈ R²(CV₁² + CV₂² − 2ρ·CV₁CV₂), with ρ = Corr(m̂₁, m̂₂) estimated from the matched pairs. Omitting it OVERSTATES the SE (usually ρ>0) and the A/A FPR falls below nominal. Also relevant to CUPED: if the covariate is centered at a POOLED mean (X̄_j − θ̂(Ȳ_j − Ȳ_pooled)), the shared Ȳ_pooled induces a small negative dependence between the adjusted arm means — O(1/n), normally ignorable, but it is a genuine violation, not an absence of one. Centering each arm at its own Ȳ_j, or at a pre-period constant, restores exact independence.

assumptions.assumption: μ₁ is bounded away from zero relative to its own standard error: g := (z_{1−α/2}·CV₁)² ≪ 1, where CV₁ = √V₁/μ₁ is the CV of the MEAN (not of the per-unit values).
assumptions.why_needed: The expansion of 1/(1+u) requires |u| < 1 with high probability; g < 1 is exactly the condition under which Fieller's set is bounded.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: At g ≥ 1 the honest confidence set is unbounded (a half-line union or the whole line). Delta and log intervals still return a finite interval and are then simply wrong: measured coverage 0.939 at CV₁=0.30 and 0.930 at CV₁=0.45 for delta-Wald, versus Fieller's 0.950 at every CV₁ tested up to 0.60.

assumptions.assumption: μ₁ > 0 (needed for the log-scale variant; needed for θ to be READABLE as a percentage in any variant).
assumptions.why_needed: log μ₁ must exist; and '+3.2%' only means what a reader thinks it means when the baseline is positive.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: If μ₁ < 0 (revenue net of refunds, a signed difference metric) θ's sign inverts relative to the absolute effect: an improvement reads as a negative percentage. The log interval is undefined. If μ₁ straddles 0 the ratio has NO moments (it is Cauchy-like — Marsaglia/Hinkley); the delta SE remains finite and is meaningless.

assumptions.assumption: V̂₁, V̂₂ are consistent for V₁, V₂ and their own sampling noise is negligible.
assumptions.why_needed: All formulas plug in V̂. At n ≥ 10⁴ this is safe.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: Use Welch-t with ν = (R̂²V̂₁+V̂₂)² / [(R̂²V̂₁)²/(n₁−1) + V̂₂²/(n₂−1)] in place of z. For binary metrics with n·p ≲ 30 prefer a score interval (Miettinen–Nurminen) over any of these.

assumptions.assumption: For the ratio-metric variant: the unit of randomization is the unit of independence, i.e. (N_i, D_i) pairs are iid ACROSS units, with arbitrary dependence WITHIN a unit.
assumptions.why_needed: The linearization Var(r̂) = Var(N − rD)/(n μ_D²) is a statement about the unit-level iid sample.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: Treating the denominator events (impressions) as the iid unit understates the variance by the design effect 1 + (E[D]−1)ρ_ICC. Measured 1.61 in a mild synthetic (Beta(2,18) per-unit CTR, D∈1..20); in production it is routinely 2–10. A/A FPR signature: nominal 0.05 becomes 0.123 at DE=1.61.

assumptions.assumption: For the ratio-metric variant: the sample (co)variance matrix of (N, D) is computed with a SINGLE consistent ddof.
assumptions.why_needed: V̂(r̂) = (S_NN − 2r̂S_ND + r̂²S_DD)/(n D̄²) is a quadratic form in (1, −r̂); non-negativity holds only if [S_NN, S_ND; S_ND, S_DD] is a genuine PSD covariance matrix.
assumptions.consequence_if_violated: Mixing ddof=0 on the squared terms with ddof=1 on the cross-moment destroys positive semidefiniteness. Verified: with N_i ≡ 0.3·D_i exactly, the correct residual variance is 0.000e+00 and the mixed-ddof form gives −5.78e−03 → NaN out of the sqrt. This is a live hazard for any engine that carries a legacy mixed-ddof convention.

derivation:
## 0. Notation

Arm j ∈ {1,2}: n_j iid units, per-unit mean μ_j, per-unit variance σ_j².
m̂_j = X̄_j, V_j := Var(m̂_j) = σ_j²/n_j, V̂_j = s_j²/n_j.

R := μ₂/μ₁, R̂ := m̂₂/m̂₁, θ = R − 1, θ̂ = R̂ − 1.
CV_j := √V_j / μ_j — **the CV of the mean**, i.e. (per-unit CV)/√n_j. This is the
quantity the question calls CV₁ = s₁/(√n₁·m̂₁). It is small: 10⁻³–10⁻¹.

w₁ := V₁/(V₁+V₂) — the control arm's share of the variance of the absolute difference.
z := z_{1−α/2}. g := z²V₁/m̂₁² = (z·CV̂₁)².

---

## 1. The delta expansion of a ratio of two means

Let g(a,b) = b/a. Then ∂g/∂a = −b/a², ∂g/∂b = 1/a. First-order Taylor about (μ₁, μ₂):

    R̂ − R ≈ (1/μ₁)(m̂₂ − μ₂) − (μ₂/μ₁²)(m̂₁ − μ₁)

so, for a general (possibly dependent) pair,

    Var(R̂) ≈ (1/μ₁²)·V₂ + (μ₂²/μ₁⁴)·V₁ − 2·(μ₂/μ₁³)·Cov(m̂₁, m̂₂).      (1)

Three terms, and each has a distinct origin:

- **(1/μ₁²)V₂** — numerator noise, scaled by the baseline. Present in every formula.
- **(μ₂²/μ₁⁴)V₁** — denominator noise. The derivative of b/a with respect to a is
  −b/a², NOT −1/a: perturbing the denominator moves the ratio by an amount
  proportional to the ratio itself. This factor of R² is the entire content of
  the question.
- **−2(μ₂/μ₁³)Cov** — the cross term, from the product of the two first-order
  perturbations. **Zero for independent arms.**

It is cleaner in relative form. Divide (1) by R²:

    Var(R̂)/R² ≈ V₁/μ₁² + V₂/μ₂² − 2Cov/(μ₁μ₂) = CV₁² + CV₂² − 2ρ·CV₁CV₂,

and since Var(θ̂) = Var(R̂) (θ̂ and R̂ differ by a constant),

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Var(θ̂) ≈ R²(CV₁² + CV₂²)      [independent arms]        │
    │          = (R²V₁ + V₂)/μ₁²                               │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Plug-in estimator and the delta ("Wald") interval:

    SÊ_θ = √(R̂²V̂₁ + V̂₂) / |m̂₁|,      CI: θ̂ ± z·SÊ_θ.            (2)

## 2. What the shortcut actually drops — and why "covariance term" is the wrong name

The shortcut is SE_Δ/m̂₁ = √(V̂₁+V̂₂)/|m̂₁|. Compare with (2):

    Var_delta / Var_short = (R̂²V̂₁ + V̂₂)/(V̂₁ + V̂₂) = 1 + (R̂² − 1)·w₁

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  SE_delta / SE_short = √(1 + (2θ̂ + θ̂²)·w₁)  ≈ 1 + θ̂·w₁  │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   (3)

(Verified algebraically over 2000 random configurations, exact to 1e-12.)

Three things follow, and the second is the one most write-ups get wrong.

**(a) The dropped piece is not a covariance.** For independent arms the cross term in
(1) is *identically zero*; there is nothing there to drop. The shortcut's error is that
it uses the **wrong coefficient on V₁** — 1 instead of R². Equivalently: the shortcut
computes Var(m̂₂ − m̂₁)/μ₁², the variance of a *difference* rescaled by a constant,
whereas the estimand is a *ratio*. Calling the omission "the covariance term" (a habit
imported from the ratio-metric case of §8, where a genuine covariance IS omitted)
predicts an error that does not exist and hides the one that does.

**(b) The shortcut does not "ignore denominator randomness" either.** It keeps V₁, with
coefficient 1, because m̂₁ appears in the numerator of the difference. A *third*, cruder
mistake — √V̂₂/|m̂₁|, genuinely holding m̂₁ fixed everywhere — drops V₁ entirely; that one
is catastrophic and loud (A/A FPR 0.166 instead of 0.05 at w₁ = 0.5). Any diagnosis must
distinguish these three formulas; they fail differently.

**(c) The error is O(θ), not O(CV₁), and it vanishes exactly at the null.** At θ = 0,
R = 1, and (3) gives exactly 1: **the shortcut is exactly the correct first-order variance
under H₀.** This is why the shortcut survives in production code — the very test bed most
likely to be pointed at it (an A/A matrix) is blind to it *by construction*.

Numerically, from (3):

| θ | w₁=0.25 | w₁=0.50 | w₁=0.75 |
|---|---|---|---|
| −0.50 | 0.901 | 0.791 | 0.661 |
| −0.20 | 0.954 | 0.906 | 0.854 |
| −0.05 | 0.988 | 0.975 | 0.963 |
| **0.00** | **1.000** | **1.000** | **1.000** |
| +0.05 | 1.013 | 1.025 | 1.038 |
| +0.10 | 1.026 | 1.051 | 1.076 |
| +0.20 | 1.054 | 1.105 | 1.153 |
| +0.50 | 1.146 | 1.275 | 1.392 |
| +1.00 | 1.323 | 1.581 | 1.803 |

The asymmetry is the practically important part: for **improvements (θ > 0) the shortcut
interval is too narrow** (anti-conservative), for **regressions (θ < 0) too wide**
(conservative, power lost). Coverage of a nominal-95% shortcut interval, which by (3)
depends only on θ and w₁ and **not at all on CV₁ or n**:

    coverage(θ) = 2Φ( z / √(1 + (2θ+θ²)w₁) ) − 1

| θ | coverage (equal-CV arms) |
|---|---|
| +0.02 | 0.948 |
| +0.05 | 0.944 |
| +0.10 | **0.939** |
| +0.20 | **0.924** |
| +0.50 | **0.904** |
| −0.20 | 0.970 |
| −0.50 | 0.987 |

Monte Carlo (10⁶ draws) reproduces these to ±0.001 and confirms the invariance in CV₁:
0.9507 / 0.9390 / 0.9052 at θ = 0 / 0.10 / 0.50 for **every** CV₁ from 0.02 to 0.45.

**When does the shortcut stop being negligible?** Set a tolerance of 0.5 percentage
points of coverage (0.945 vs 0.950): that is |θ|·w₁ ≳ 0.05, i.e. **|θ| ≳ 10% at
w₁ = 0.5**. A shipped 3% lift is a ~0.3% SE error — genuinely negligible. A 30% lift on
a small-base metric is a 15% SE error and a 92% interval sold as 95%.

## 3. Second order: bias, and the actual role of CV₁

Write m̂₁ = μ₁(1+u), m̂₂ = μ₂(1+v), E[u]=E[v]=0, Var(u)=CV₁², Var(v)=CV₂².

    R̂ = R(1+v)(1 − u + u² − u³ + …) = R[1 + (v − u) + (u² − uv) + O(3)]

Taking expectations (independent, so E[uv]=0):

    ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
    │  E[θ̂] − θ ≈ (1 + θ)·CV₁²         │   (4)
    └──────────────────────────────────┘

Empirically (2×10⁶ draws): CV₁=0.05, θ=0 → +0.00255 vs predicted +0.00250; CV₁=0.10,
θ=0.20 → +0.01255 vs predicted +0.01200. (Deteriorates past CV₁≈0.2 as the third-order
term bites.)

Two readings of (4), and they point in opposite directions:

- **In SE units the bias is negligible**: bias/SE ≈ CV₁²/√(CV₁²+CV₂²) ≈ CV₁/√2. At
  CV₁ = 0.1 that is 0.07 SE — invisible to coverage. So bias is *not* what limits the
  delta method.
- **Relative to the effect it can be large**: bias/θ ≈ CV₁²/θ. At CV₁ = 0.05 the bias is
  +0.25 percentage points of relative effect; on a true +1% lift that is a 25%
  overstatement of the headline number, systematically upward, and it does not average
  out across a portfolio of experiments. If the organization aggregates reported lifts,
  correct it: θ̂_bc = R̂(1 − CV̂₁²) − 1.

What CV₁ *does* limit is the normal approximation itself, through the pole at m̂₁ = 0.
P(m̂₁ ≤ 0) ≈ Φ(−1/CV₁): 3e−7 at CV₁=0.2, 1.3e−3 at CV₁=0.33, 2.5% at CV₁=0.5. The
classical rule of thumb (Cochran, Sampling Techniques §6.6) is that the ratio estimator's
normal approximation is trustworthy when the denominator's CV is below ~0.1; Fieller
makes the boundary precise: bounded interval ⟺ g < 1 ⟺ **CV₁ < 1/z ≈ 0.51** at α=0.05.

Realistic regimes for this engine:
- conversion p=10⁻³, n=10⁵ ⇒ np=100 ⇒ CV₁ = √((1−p)/np) ≈ 0.10 ⇒ g = 0.038. Real.
- revenue/user, per-unit CV 5–20, n=10⁵ ⇒ CV₁ = 0.016–0.063 ⇒ g ≤ 0.015. Marginal.
- any metric at n=10⁷ ⇒ CV₁ ≲ 0.006 ⇒ g ≲ 1e−4. Irrelevant.

## 4. The three intervals are three classical test forms

This is the organizing idea, and it explains every empirical result below.

- **Shortcut**, √(V̂₁+V̂₂)/|m̂₁|: variance evaluated **at the null R = 1**. For testing
  H₀: θ = 0 it is therefore the *score-type* test — and exactly right there.
- **Delta (2)**, √(R̂²V̂₁+V̂₂)/|m̂₁|: variance evaluated **at the estimate R̂**. A *Wald*
  test. Wald tests are famously non-invariant to reparameterization (Vaeth 1985;
  Dagenais & Dufour 1991) — testing μ₂−μ₁=0 and μ₂/μ₁−1=0, the same hypothesis, gives
  two different p-values.
- **Fieller**: variance evaluated **at each hypothesized R**, then inverted. The score
  test *for every R*, not just at the null.

## 5. Fieller's theorem

For a candidate value R, the statistic m̂₂ − R·m̂₁ has mean 0 and variance
V₂ + R²V₁ − 2R·V₁₂ (= V₂ + R²V₁ for independent arms) — **exactly**, no approximation,
under joint normality. Invert the test:

    { R : (m̂₂ − R·m̂₁)² ≤ z²(V̂₂ + R²V̂₁) }

which is the quadratic A·R² − 2B·R + C ≤ 0 with

    A = m̂₁² − z²V̂₁,     B = m̂₁m̂₂ − z²V̂₁₂  (= m̂₁m̂₂ if independent),     C = m̂₂² − z²V̂₂
    disc = B² − AC = z²( m̂₁²V̂₂ + m̂₂²V̂₁ − z²V̂₁V̂₂ )   [independent case]

**Branches (all three must be implemented):**

1. **A > 0 and disc > 0** — bounded interval, R ∈ [(B−√disc)/A, (B+√disc)/A].
   Closed form (independent arms), which makes the relation to the delta interval exact:

        R ∈ ( 1/(1−g) )·[ R̂ ± (z/|m̂₁|)·√( R̂²V̂₁ + (1−g)V̂₂ ) ] ,   g = z²V̂₁/m̂₁²

   (verified equal to the root form to 1e-10). As g → 0 this is **exactly** the delta
   interval (2): Fieller = delta + O(g) corrections, namely a center inflated by
   1/(1−g) and a half-width inflated by roughly 1/(1−g). The center shift is *not* a
   bias correction — it moves the same direction as the bias (4) — it is the geometry
   of the confidence set.
2. **A ≤ 0, disc > 0** — the parabola opens downward: the set is the **exclusive union**
   (−∞, r_lo] ∪ [r_hi, ∞), i.e. the complement of an interval. Occurs when the
   denominator is not significantly different from zero (|m̂₁| ≤ z·SE(m̂₁)).
3. **A ≤ 0, disc ≤ 0** — the whole real line. "No information about the relative effect."

Branch 1 fires with probability 1 − Φ(−1/CV₁)-ish; measured share of non-bounded outcomes:
0% at CV₁ ≤ 0.10, 0.12% at 0.20, **8.5% at 0.30**, **39.7% at 0.45**, 61.5% at 0.60.

**Fieller has exact coverage.** With all three branches handled, measured coverage was
0.9500 ± 0.0002 at *every* combination of CV₁ ∈ {0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60}
and θ ∈ {0, 0.5} (10⁶ draws each). Delta over the same grid: 0.950 → 0.949 → 0.939 →
0.930. Shortcut: 0.951 at θ=0 but 0.904 at θ=0.5 at *every* CV₁.

**This is not a lucky implementation — it is a theorem.** Gleser & Hwang (1987, Ann.
Statist. 15:1351) proved that for a ratio of normal means *any* confidence procedure with
guaranteed level 1−α must produce unbounded sets with positive probability. Delta and log
intervals are always finite; therefore their guaranteed coverage is 0, i.e. their coverage
is not uniform over the parameter space and there is always a region (small |μ₁|) where
they fail arbitrarily badly. Fieller's unbounded branch is not a defect to be patched — it
is the only honest answer available, and it is the reason Fieller attains nominal coverage
where the others cannot.

**The coherence identity.** At R = 1 the Fieller inequality reads
(m̂₂ − m̂₁)² ≤ z²(V̂₁ + V̂₂). Therefore:

    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Fieller's CI for θ excludes 0  ⟺  the two-sample test of         │
    │  μ₂ − μ₁ = 0 rejects at level α.  Identically. Always.            │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Fieller's p-value for H₀: θ=0 IS the absolute difference's p-value. The shortcut shares
this property (its variance is also the null variance at R=1) — that is its one real
virtue. The delta/Wald interval does **not**: it can include 0 while the absolute test
rejects, and vice versa, producing a report in which "the absolute effect is significant"
and "the relative CI contains 0" appear side by side about the same comparison.

Because Fieller is a test inversion, it composes with anything that supplies a critical
radius: replace z by the two-tier/Bonferroni/BH-effective quantile, or by an always-valid
confidence-sequence boundary, and the construction is unchanged.

**Engineering consequence (important).** Fieller's half-width is *not* z × a stored SE:
g depends on α. An interface that recomputes intervals at many α values from a cached SE
(an alpha slider) must recompute Fieller from (m̂₁, m̂₂, V̂₁, V̂₂, α) — cheap, closed form,
but not a rescale. Any code path that multiplies a stored half-width by z_new/z_old is
silently producing a delta interval.

## 6. Is a symmetric-in-θ interval the right shape at all? — the log scale

θ is not symmetric under swapping arms: θ_{2vs1} = R − 1 while θ_{1vs2} = 1/R − 1 =
−θ/(1+θ). A "+100%" and a "−50%" are the same experiment reported from opposite ends. An
interval symmetric in θ therefore maps to an asymmetric one when the arms are swapped —
the analysis depends on which arm you called control, which is not a property any
statistical procedure should have.

On the log scale λ = log R = log μ₂ − log μ₁:

    Var(λ̂) ≈ CV₁² + CV₂²  (independent),   CI:  λ̂ ± z√(CV̂₁² + CV̂₂²)
    θ ∈ [ exp(λ̂ − z c) − 1 ,  exp(λ̂ + z c) − 1 ],  c = √(V̂₁/m̂₁² + V̂₂/m̂₂²)

Properties: (i) exactly equivariant under arm swap (λ ↔ −λ), (ii) cannot produce
θ ≤ −1, which is impossible when both means are positive and which the delta interval
happily returns, (iii) agrees with the delta interval to first order (verified: relative
difference in half-width 1.2e−10 at CV ≈ 1e−5), (iv) measured coverage 0.950–0.955 up to
CV₁=0.10, then **over**-covers: 0.974 at CV₁=0.20, 0.994 at 0.30. Log is conservative
where delta is anti-conservative. (v) It is still a Wald test — on a different
parameterization — so it too breaks the p-value coherence identity of §5.

For binary metrics this is the textbook relative-risk interval, Var(log RR) =
(1−p₁)/(n₁p₁) + (1−p₂)/(n₂p₂) (Katz et al. 1978), which any implementation must reproduce
exactly.

## 7. Small, near-zero, or negative μ₁

Detection is available from sufficient statistics alone, via g = z²V̂₁/m̂₁² = (z·CV̂₁)²:

- **g ≥ 1** (|m̂₁| ≤ z·SE(m̂₁)): no bounded relative interval exists at level α. Report
  the relative effect as unbounded / undefined and fall back to the absolute effect.
  Fieller reaches this conclusion automatically; delta and log must be gated explicitly.
- **0.05 ≲ g < 1** (CV₁ ≳ 0.11): the Fieller correction exceeds ~5% of the width. Warn
  and prefer Fieller.
- **m̂₁ < 0**: θ is defined but its sign is inverted relative to intuition, and it is
  discontinuous through 0 — an experiment that moves μ₁ from −0.01 to +0.01 produces a
  relative effect of −200%. Recommend suppressing the relative effect entirely for
  sign-indefinite metrics and reporting only the absolute effect. If a normalized
  quantity is demanded, use a **symmetric** one, Δ/((m̂₁+m̂₂)/2) ∈ [−2, 2], and label it
  as a different estimand — it is not (μ₂−μ₁)/μ₁.
- **Both means near zero**: the ratio of two centered normals is Cauchy (Marsaglia 1965;
  Hinkley 1969) — no mean, no variance. The delta SE is a finite number computed from a
  distribution with no second moment.

## 8. The ratio metric (clicks per impression) — a genuinely different case

Estimand per arm: r = E[N]/E[D] (equivalently ΣN/ΣD), **not** E[N/D]. These differ:
measured 0.10026 vs 0.10006 in a synthetic — small here, but they are different
population quantities and E[N/D] is undefined for units with D=0.

**Linearization.** With Z_i := N_i − r·D_i (E[Z] = 0 by construction):

    r̂ − r = (N̄ − r D̄)/D̄ = Z̄/D̄ ≈ Z̄/μ_D
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Var(r̂) ≈ Var(Z)/(n μ_D²) = (σ_N² − 2r σ_ND + r² σ_D²)/(n μ_D²) │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    V̂(r̂) = (S_NN − 2r̂ S_ND + r̂² S_DD) / (n D̄²)

Sufficient statistics required per arm: n, ΣN, ΣD, ΣN², ΣD², **ΣND**. The cross-moment is
mandatory, not optional. Verified against a 400-replicate unit-level bootstrap oracle:
linearized SE 2.6254e−04 vs bootstrap 2.6337e−04 (ratio 0.997).

**How this differs from the ratio-of-arm-means case — the point of the exercise:**

1. **Here the covariance term is real, first-order, and nonzero at the null.** N_i and D_i
   are correlated within a unit by construction (a user with more impressions has more
   clicks). Dropping −2r·S_ND is a *first-order* error that does not vanish anywhere in
   the parameter space. Measured inflation: SE ×1.20 (heterogeneous CTR) to ×1.31
   (homogeneous). A/A FPR signature: nominal 0.05 → **0.019** (×1.20) or **0.010**
   (×1.31) — grossly conservative, loudly visible, and the exact opposite of the
   between-arms case where the analogous-sounding term is exactly zero and dropping it
   changes nothing at the null. One name, two entirely different objects.
2. **The unit of independence is the unit, not the denominator event.** Impression-level
   binomial variance r(1−r)/ΣD understates by the design effect 1 + (E[D]−1)ρ_ICC —
   measured 1.61, so SE ×0.787, A/A FPR **0.123**. This is the canonical industrial error
   (Deng, Knoblich & Lu, KDD 2018; Kohavi, Tang & Xu 2020, ch. 18).
3. **Composition to a relative effect is a ratio of ratios.** ψ = r₂/r₁ − 1, arms
   independent ⇒ Var(ψ̂) ≈ (r₂/r₁)²(c₁² + c₂²) with c_j² := V̂(r̂_j)/r̂_j². Everything in
   §1–§6 applies verbatim with (m̂₁, m̂₂, V̂₁, V̂₂) → (r̂₁, r̂₂, V̂(r̂₁), V̂(r̂₂)), including
   Fieller. Expanded, c_j² = (CV_{N,j}² + CV_{D,j}² − 2ρ_j CV_{N,j} CV_{D,j})/n_j — the
   same three-term shape as (1), now *within* an arm.
4. **The near-zero-denominator hazard is milder within an arm** (D_i ≥ 0, bounded below
   for enrolled units, so CV_D is tiny; measured c₁ = 0.0085 ⇒ g = 2.8e−4, Fieller
   correction negligible) but is **unchanged between arms** if r₁ itself is rare.
5. **Units with D_i = 0 must be kept.** They contribute Z_i = N_i (= 0 if N is nested in
   D) and correctly enter n and D̄. Dropping them is a post-randomization filter and
   biases the estimand.
6. **Storage note.** Per-unit second moments are not day-additive: ΣᵢN_i² over a
   cumulative window cannot be assembled from daily ΣᵢN_i². The additive state must be
   per-(unit, day) N and D **sums**; the squares and cross-products are formed only after
   summing over days per unit. Anything else silently computes the within-day variance.

## 9. Recommendation

Report **Fieller** as the relative-effect interval, with the delta-Wald SE (2) exposed
separately as the SE field for MDE/power/BI, and the p-value taken from the absolute
two-sample test (which §5 shows is Fieller's own p-value).

Rationale, in order of weight:
1. **Coherence.** H₀: θ = 0 and H₀: μ₂ − μ₁ = 0 are one hypothesis; only Fieller and the
   shortcut give them one p-value. The delta/Wald interval can contradict the p-value
   printed next to it.
2. **Exact coverage** under the normality the CLT already supplies, uniformly in CV₁ —
   0.9500 measured at every CV₁ up to 0.60, where delta drifts to 0.930 and log to 0.994.
3. **Honest degradation.** Gleser–Hwang says a finite interval cannot be right near
   μ₁ = 0; Fieller is the procedure that says so instead of guessing.
4. **Cheap change control.** Because Fieller's rejection set at θ=0 is *identical* to the
   shortcut's, replacing a shortcut with Fieller **cannot move a single A/A false
   positive**. Interval endpoints move (by O(θ·w₁) and O(g)); decisions at the null do
   not. That is an unusually clean version bump: the numbers that change are exactly the
   ones that were wrong, and the FPR invariance is provable rather than merely measured.

Costs, stated plainly: three branches to implement instead of one; a non-symmetric
interval, so "estimate ± half-width" is no longer a valid rendering; and the half-width is
not proportional to z, so α-inversion must recompute rather than rescale.

If a symmetric interval is architecturally mandatory, the second-best is the **log-scale**
interval (equivariant under arm swap, cannot emit θ < −1, conservative rather than
anti-conservative where it fails), guarded by g < 1 and by μ̂₁ > 0 — and then the p-value
must continue to come from the absolute test, not from the interval.

The one option to retire is the shortcut: it is exactly right at the null, which is
precisely why nothing in the test suite will ever notice that it under-covers every
result the experiment was run to find.

recommended.name: Fieller interval (inverted score test) for R = μ₂/μ₁, reported as θ = R − 1
recommended.point_estimate: θ̂ = m̂₂/m̂₁ − 1.  Optional bias correction θ̂_bc = R̂(1 − CV̂₁²) − 1, worth applying when CV̂₁ > 0.03 and results are aggregated across experiments.
recommended.standard_error: SÊ_θ = √(R̂²·V̂₁ + V̂₂) / |m̂₁|,  with V̂_j = s_j²/n_j and R̂ = m̂₂/m̂₁.  Equivalently SÊ_θ = |R̂|·√(CV̂₁² + CV̂₂²).  Reported for MDE/power/BI only — it is NOT half the interval width under the recommended interval, and that must be documented.  (Paired mode: add −2R̂·V̂₁₂ inside the radical.)
recommended.interval:
Let z = z_{1−α/2} at the EFFECTIVE per-comparison α, and A = m̂₁² − z²V̂₁, B = m̂₁m̂₂ − z²V̂₁₂ (B = m̂₁m̂₂ for independent arms), C = m̂₂² − z²V̂₂, disc = B² − AC.
  • A > 0 and disc > 0 → θ ∈ [(B − √disc)/A − 1, (B + √disc)/A − 1].  Equivalently, with g = z²V̂₁/m̂₁²:  θ ∈ [R̂ ± (z/|m̂₁|)√(R̂²V̂₁ + (1−g)V̂₂)]/(1−g) − 1.
  • A ≤ 0 and disc > 0 → unbounded: the complement of an interval, (−∞, r_lo] ∪ [r_hi, ∞).  Emit 'relative effect unbounded at this α'.
  • A ≤ 0 and disc ≤ 0 → (−∞, +∞).
For n < ~200 per arm replace z by t_{ν,1−α/2} with Welch ν = (R̂²V̂₁+V̂₂)²/[(R̂²V̂₁)²/(n₁−1) + V̂₂²/(n₂−1)].  For an always-valid readout replace z by the confidence-sequence radius; the inversion is unchanged.
recommended.pvalue: p = 2(1 − Φ(|m̂₂ − m̂₁| / √(V̂₁ + V̂₂))) — i.e. exactly the absolute two-sample (Welch) p-value.  This is not a convenience substitution: Fieller's own test of R = 1 reduces algebraically to precisely this statistic, so the relative CI excludes 0 if and only if p < α.
recommended.rationale: It is the only one of the candidates that (i) assigns one p-value to what is one hypothesis, so the relative interval can never contradict the absolute test printed beside it; (ii) attains exact nominal coverage under the normality the CLT already provides — measured 0.9500 at every CV₁ from 0.05 to 0.60 and every θ tested, where the delta/Wald interval drifts to 0.930 and the shortcut to 0.904; (iii) degrades honestly to an unbounded set exactly when Gleser–Hwang (1987) says no finite interval can be correct; and (iv) is a drop-in for a shortcut implementation under change control, because its rejection set at θ = 0 is bitwise identical to the shortcut's — so the A/A false-positive matrix is provably invariant and only the interval endpoints move.

alternatives.name: Delta / Wald interval (variance at the estimate)
alternatives.when_preferable: When the architecture requires a symmetric 'estimate ± z·SE' interval whose half-width scales with z (so a stored SE can be re-inverted at any α), and CV₁ < 0.10 is enforced. It is the g → 0 limit of Fieller and agrees with it to O(g).
alternatives.cost: Wald non-invariance: it produces a second, different p-value for the same null, so the relative CI can include 0 while the absolute test rejects. Under A/A its total FPR is ≈ nominal but its false positives are asymmetric in sign (see discriminating predictions). Coverage degrades with CV₁ (0.949 at 0.20, 0.939 at 0.30, 0.930 at 0.45) and it returns a finite interval even when |m̂₁| < z·SE(m̂₁), where none exists.

alternatives.name: Log-ratio (Wald on log R)
alternatives.when_preferable: Positive-by-construction metrics (conversion, revenue with no refunds, any count rate) where equivariance under swapping the arms matters and a bounded, multiplicatively symmetric interval is wanted. For binary metrics this is the standard Katz relative-risk interval, so it is also the interoperability choice.
alternatives.cost: Undefined for μ̂₁ ≤ 0 or μ̂₂ ≤ 0, which is precisely the regime that needs help. Still a Wald test, so it also breaks the p-value coherence identity. Over-covers where delta under-covers (measured 0.974 at CV₁=0.20, 0.994 at 0.30) — safer, but it buys that safety with power, and the over-coverage is not controlled.

alternatives.name: Shortcut: SE of the absolute difference divided by the baseline
alternatives.when_preferable: Only as a deliberate documented approximation when |θ| is guaranteed small (< 5%) — e.g. a mature product where every shipped effect is sub-percent. Its one genuine virtue is that, like Fieller, it never disagrees with the absolute test's p-value.
alternatives.cost: Coverage error is a function of the true effect size and w₁ = V₁/(V₁+V₂) and is independent of n: 0.939 at θ=+10%, 0.924 at +20%, 0.904 at +50%. Directionally asymmetric — too narrow for improvements, too wide for regressions — so it over-states confidence in exactly the results that get shipped. Invisible to any A/A test by construction.

alternatives.name: Score interval with null-constrained variance (Miettinen–Nurminen / Koopman) — binary metrics only
alternatives.formula: Invert { R : (p̂₂ − R·p̂₁)² ≤ z²·[ p̃₂(1−p̃₂)/n₂ + R²·p̃₁(1−p̃₁)/n₁ ]·κ }, where p̃_j are the MLEs of p₁, p₂ constrained to p₂ = R·p₁, and κ = N/(N−1) is the small-sample correction.
alternatives.when_preferable: Binary conversion metrics with small event counts (n·p ≲ 30 in either arm), where the unconstrained variance plug-in that Fieller uses is itself unreliable. Best-documented coverage in the risk-ratio literature.
alternatives.cost: Requires a constrained MLE (a closed-form cubic root or a one-dimensional solve) rather than a formula in the sufficient statistics; it is metric-family-specific, so it violates a 'methods are plugins, nothing special-cases a metric shape' design rule. At n ≥ 10⁴ it agrees with Fieller to O(1/n) and buys nothing.

alternatives.name: Bootstrap (BCa) or a bootstrapped-t on the ratio, over units
alternatives.formula: Resample units within arm, recompute θ̂* = m̂₂*/m̂₁* − 1, take BCa percentiles.
alternatives.when_preferable: Heavy-tailed revenue where the CLT itself — not the ratio structure — is the binding constraint (skewness γ with n < 25γ²), and for ratio metrics as an independent oracle for the linearized variance (used exactly that way in the checks above: linearized SE 2.6254e−04 vs bootstrap 2.6337e−04).
alternatives.cost: Needs the raw per-unit vectors, which the sufficient-statistics design does not retain — it changes what the engine must store and cannot be run at every cumulative cutoff. BCa is also unstable when m̂₁* can approach 0, which is the same failure mode, unpatched. Best used as an offline calibration oracle, not as the reported interval.

finite_sample_behavior:
Three separate finite-sample effects, in decreasing order of importance for this engine's n:

(1) **Ratio non-normality (governed by CV₁, the CV of the mean).** The delta and log intervals are first-order; their coverage error is O(g) = O((z·CV₁)²). Measured coverage of the nominal-95% delta interval, V known, equal-CV arms, 10⁶ draws: 0.9508 (CV₁=0.02), 0.9516 (0.05), 0.9516 (0.10), 0.9487 (0.20), 0.9388 (0.30), 0.9299 (0.45) — and this is essentially independent of θ. Fieller is exact at all of these (0.9498–0.9504). The share of samples at which no bounded interval exists rises 0% → 0.12% → 8.5% → 39.7% at CV₁ = 0.10 → 0.20 → 0.30 → 0.45.

(2) **Shortcut error (governed by θ and w₁, not by n).** Coverage 2Φ(z/√(1+(2θ+θ²)w₁))−1: 0.9507/0.9390/0.9052 at θ = 0/0.10/0.50, identical at every CV₁ from 0.02 to 0.45. This does NOT shrink as n grows — it is a first-order misspecification, not a finite-sample artifact, and an engine that assumes 'n is large so approximations are fine' will never outgrow it.

(3) **Noise in V̂ and non-normality of the underlying data.** At n ≥ 10⁴ the V̂ noise contributes O(1/n) and is dominated by (1) and (2); use Welch-t below ~200/arm. The CLT error itself is the binding constraint for heavy-tailed revenue: Cochran's rule n > 25γ² (γ = per-unit skewness) for accurate one-sided 5% rates. At γ = 20 (a plausible revenue-per-user figure with a long tail) that demands n > 10⁴ per arm before any of this analysis applies. The engine cannot compute γ from n, Σx, Σx² — storing Σx³ would let it warn.

Bias: E[θ̂] − θ ≈ (1+θ)CV₁², confirmed empirically (CV₁=0.05, θ=0: +0.00255 vs +0.00250 predicted; CV₁=0.10, θ=0.20: +0.01255 vs +0.01200). Negligible in SE units (≈CV₁/√2) but not relative to a small true effect (bias/θ ≈ CV₁²/θ), and always upward.

Cumulative recomputation: CV₁ is largest at the earliest cutoffs, so every one of these errors is worst at the start of an experiment and decays as 1/√n. An engine that recomputes at many cutoffs will therefore see the delta/Fieller divergence and the unbounded branch concentrated in the first few looks — which is exactly where a peeking operator looks hardest.
failure_modes: μ̂₁ within z·SE of zero (g ≥ 1): no bounded interval exists at level α. Delta and log return a finite interval anyway with arbitrarily bad coverage; Fieller returns the correct unbounded set. Gate on g = z²V̂₁/m̂₁² and refuse rather than guess.

μ̂₁ < 0 (revenue net of refunds, signed-difference metrics): θ's sign inverts relative to the absolute effect and θ is discontinuous through μ₁ = 0. Suppress the relative effect; report the absolute one. Note that |m̂₁| in the denominator of the SE is required to keep the SE positive, but that does NOT fix the sign inversion of θ̂ itself.
Both means near zero: the ratio is Cauchy-like with no moments (Marsaglia/Hinkley). Every SE formula here returns a finite number that describes nothing.

Large true effects (|θ| ≳ 20%): the shortcut's interval is off by ~10% of its width — too narrow for wins, too wide for losses. Most damaging on new-surface or low-base metrics where genuine 30–100% lifts occur.
Small denominators in ratio metrics: units with D_i = 0 must be retained (dropping them is a post-randomization filter and biases the estimand). Guard only the arm-level D̄ = 0 case.
Ratio metric with the within-unit cross-moment omitted: SE inflated ×1.20–1.31, A/A FPR collapses to 0.019–0.010 against a nominal 0.05. Conservative, so it looks 'safe' and quietly destroys power.
Ratio metric computed at the denominator-event level (per impression rather than per unit): SE understated by √(design effect); at DE = 1.61 the A/A FPR is 0.123 against nominal 0.05.

Mixed ddof across S_NN, S_DD, S_ND in the ratio-metric variance: the quadratic form loses positive semidefiniteness and can return a negative variance (verified: −5.78e−03 in the exactly-proportional case). Yields NaN from sqrt, or worse, a tiny positive number after a clamp.

Heavy-tailed data with n below Cochran's 25γ²: the CLT has not engaged, and choosing between Fieller/delta/log is rearranging deck chairs. Only a bootstrap over units (which needs the raw vectors) or a much larger n helps.

Multiplicity/α-inversion with Fieller: the half-width is not proportional to z because g depends on α. A cached-SE-times-new-z code path silently degrades to a delta interval at every α except the one it was computed at.
Paired mode: Cov(m̂₁, m̂₂) ≠ 0 and the cross term −2R·V̂₁₂ is first-order. Omitting it (usually ρ > 0) overstates the SE and depresses the A/A FPR below nominal.

CUPED with a pooled covariate mean: the shared Ȳ_pooled makes the two adjusted arm means dependent, so the 'independent arms' zero-covariance claim is O(1/n) false. Center per-arm or at a pre-period constant to restore it exactly.

known_answer_tests.setup: m̂₁ = m̂₂ (exactly zero observed effect), any V̂₁, V̂₂.
known_answer_tests.expected: SE_delta == SE_shortcut exactly (bitwise, up to fp reassociation). Fieller's interval is symmetric about 0 in θ and contains 0.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: Pins the R̂² coefficient at its null value. A test that only checks the null cannot distinguish shortcut from delta — which is the whole trap; use this as a REGRESSION anchor, never as evidence of correctness.

known_answer_tests.setup: V̂₁ = 0 (deterministic control mean), V̂₂ > 0, any m̂₁ ≠ m̂₂.
known_answer_tests.expected: SE_delta == SE_shortcut == √V̂₂/|m̂₁| exactly, and Fieller == delta exactly (g = 0, so 1/(1−g) = 1).
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: Isolates w₁ = 0. Any implementation that differs here has an error unrelated to the ratio structure.

known_answer_tests.expected: SE_delta / SE_shortcut == R̂ == 2 exactly. Generally the ratio is |R̂| when V̂₂ = 0.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: The sharpest possible discriminator between the two formulas — a factor of 2, not a percentage. Also catches the third wrong formula √V̂₂/|m̂₁|, which returns 0 here.

known_answer_tests.setup: Any (m̂₁, m̂₂, V̂₁, V̂₂) with m̂₁ > z√V̂₁. Compare 'Fieller interval excludes θ=0' against '(m̂₂−m̂₁)² > z²(V̂₁+V̂₂)'.
known_answer_tests.expected: Identical boolean, for every input, always. Same for the shortcut interval. NOT identical for the delta interval.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: This is the coherence identity of §5 and it is exact, not asymptotic — verified over 2000 random configurations. It is the single cheapest test that tells you which of the three formulas is implemented, and it will fail on a delta implementation at inputs near the boundary.

known_answer_tests.expected: The Fieller set is a half-line, not a division-by-zero. Implementation must return ±inf on one side, not NaN or a crash.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: A = 0 is the exact hinge of the quadratic and the branch most implementations omit. In floating point A can also land at ±1e-18, flipping between the bounded and complement branches — the code must select the branch on sign(A) with the same tolerance used everywhere else.

known_answer_tests.expected: The solution set is the EXCLUSIVE union (−∞, r_lo] ∪ [r_hi, ∞) — the complement of an interval — not the interval [r_lo, r_hi].
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: Dividing the roots by a negative A silently reverses their order. An implementation that sorts the roots and returns [min, max] as the CI returns the exact complement of the truth: a narrow, confident-looking interval around a value the data excludes. Coverage collapses toward 0 rather than degrading gently. Verified: with this branch counted correctly, Fieller coverage is 0.9499–0.9504 at CV₁ = 0.30/0.45/0.60; counted as a plain interval it is badly wrong.

known_answer_tests.setup: Binary metric: n₁ = n₂ = n, successes k₁, k₂. Compare the log-scale interval against the textbook Katz relative-risk interval, Var(log RR) = (1−p̂₁)/(n₁p̂₁) + (1−p̂₂)/(n₂p̂₂).
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: An independent, universally published external anchor for the whole construction. Also catches the ddof convention on a Bernoulli variance (p̂(1−p̂)·n/(n−1) vs p̂(1−p̂)), which shifts the interval by a factor (n−1)/n that no internal test would notice.

known_answer_tests.setup: Ratio metric with D_i ≡ 1 for all units.
known_answer_tests.expected: The ratio-metric machinery reduces EXACTLY to the mean case: S_DD = 0, S_ND = 0, D̄ = 1, so V̂(r̂) = S_NN/n.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: Proves the ratio path and the mean path are the same estimator, so any subsequent divergence between the two code paths is a bug, not a modeling choice.

known_answer_tests.setup: Ratio metric with N_i = c·D_i exactly for every unit (perfect proportionality), c = 0.3.
known_answer_tests.expected: r̂ = 0.3 exactly and V̂(r̂) = 0 exactly; the CI is a point.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: The residual Z_i = N_i − rD_i is identically zero, so this is the sharpest possible test that the cross term is subtracted with the right sign AND the right ddof. Verified: consistent ddof gives 0.000e+00; ddof=0 on the squares with ddof=1 on the cross term gives −5.78e−03, i.e. a NEGATIVE variance.

known_answer_tests.setup: Arm-swap equivariance: compute the interval for (arm1, arm2) and for (arm2, arm1).
known_answer_tests.expected: The log-scale interval maps exactly: [lo, hi] for R ⟹ [1/hi, 1/lo] for 1/R. Fieller likewise (it is a set in R, and the map R ↦ 1/R is exact). The delta and shortcut intervals do NOT.
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: Pins a structural property no amount of coverage simulation reveals, and documents in a test which formula is deliberately non-equivariant.

known_answer_tests.setup: α-inversion: compute the Fieller interval at α = 0.05 and at α = 0.01 from the same sufficient statistics; compare against half-width(0.05)·z_{0.995}/z_{0.975}.
known_answer_tests.expected: They must DIFFER, by a factor involving (1−g₀.₀₅)/(1−g₀.₀₁).
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: The only test that catches an alpha-slider or two-tier-correction path that rescales a cached half-width — which silently converts Fieller into delta at every α but the cached one.

known_answer_tests.setup: Degenerate: V̂₁ = V̂₂ = 0 with m̂₁ ≠ m̂₂; and n₁ = 1.
known_answer_tests.expected: Zero-width interval at θ̂ (not NaN); and a documented refusal for n₁ = 1 rather than a divide-by-zero in s².
known_answer_tests.why_it_bites: The engine recomputes at early cutoffs where an arm may have one or zero units; these branches are reached in production long before any statistician looks at them.

common_implementation_errors: SE_Δ/m̂₁ (the shortcut): coefficient 1 instead of R̂² on V̂₁. Signature — SE ratio is exactly |R̂| when V̂₂ = 0; coverage 0.939/0.924/0.904 at θ = +10%/+20%/+50% and 0.970/0.987 at −20%/−50%, INDEPENDENT of CV₁ and n; A/A FPR exactly nominal, so no null-based test can see it.

√V̂₂/|m̂₁| — genuinely holding m̂₁ constant everywhere and dropping V̂₁ entirely. Signature: A/A FPR 0.166 against nominal 0.05 at w₁ = 0.5 (coverage 0.834). Loud; do not confuse this failure with the shortcut's, which is silent at the null.

Delta-Wald where a score/Fieller interval was intended. Signature: total A/A FPR ≈ nominal but the false positives are asymmetric in sign — left-tail share ≈ 0.5 + φ(z)z²·CV₁·√w₁/α, i.e. 0.66 at CV₁=0.05 and 0.83 at CV₁=0.10 (α=0.05), versus a measured 0.50 for shortcut and Fieller. Also: the relative CI and the printed p-value disagree near the boundary.

Sorting the two Fieller roots and returning [min, max] when A < 0. The true set is the complement. Signature: a suspiciously tight interval when the control mean is barely significant, and coverage that collapses rather than degrades.

Using m̂₁ rather than |m̂₁| in the SE denominator: for m̂₁ < 0 the 'half-width' is negative and the returned interval has lo > hi. Signature: an interval that silently contains everything or nothing depending on how downstream code compares the endpoints.

Reusing a cached half-width and rescaling by z when α changes (two-tier correction, BH, an alpha slider). Correct for delta and log; WRONG for Fieller, because g = (z·CV̂₁)² depends on α. Signature: the interval matches Fieller at exactly one α and is a delta interval at every other.

Computing CV₁ from the per-unit CV (s₁/m̂₁) instead of the mean's CV (s₁/(√n₁·m̂₁)). Signature: g inflated by n₁, so every relative interval is declared unbounded — or, with the reciprocal error, the guard never fires.
Ratio metric: omitting the −2r̂·S_ND term. Signature: A/A FPR 0.019 (SE ×1.20) to 0.010 (SE ×1.31) against nominal 0.05 — conservative, so it survives review as 'safe'.
Ratio metric: variance computed at the denominator-event level, r̂(1−r̂)/ΣD. Signature: A/A FPR 0.123 at a design effect of 1.61; scales with E[D] and with the between-unit heterogeneity of the rate.

Ratio metric: mixed ddof between the squared and cross terms. Signature: negative variance in the near-proportional case (measured −5.78e−03 where the truth is exactly 0) → NaN, or a clamped near-zero SE and an absurdly significant result.

Ratio metric: estimating E[N/D] (mean of per-unit ratios) instead of E[N]/E[D]. A different estimand (0.10006 vs 0.10026 in a mild synthetic; the gap grows with heterogeneity) and undefined for D_i = 0.
Percentage scaling applied twice, or applied to the endpoints but not the SE. Signature: an interval 100× too wide, or a reported SE inconsistent with the reported width by exactly 100.

Applying the relative-effect construction to a metric whose mean can be ≤ 0 without a guard. Signature: sign-inverted lifts and, when μ₁ ≈ 0, interval widths spanning thousands of percent that pass every finite-value check.
Paired mode reusing the independent-arms formula (V̂₁₂ = 0). Signature: A/A FPR below nominal in proportion to the pairing correlation; the more effective the pairing, the more power is thrown away.
discriminating_predictions: A/A FPR alone CANNOT distinguish the shortcut from Fieller: their rejection sets for H₀: θ=0 are algebraically identical, so the measured FPRs must agree to the last false positive, not merely within Monte Carlo noise (confirmed: 0.05008/0.04995/0.05002/0.04987/0.04984/0.04998 at CV₁ = 0.005…0.20, bitwise the same reject set). If a matrix reports any difference between two implementations that both claim to be one of these, at least one is neither. Corollary: a change from shortcut to Fieller is provably FPR-neutral, which makes it a cheap change-control step.

The delta/Wald interval is identified by the SIGN SPLIT of A/A false positives, with no non-null effect needed. Predicted left-tail share ≈ 0.5 + φ(z)·z²·CV₁·√w₁/α; at α=0.05, w₁=0.5 that is 0.5 + 3.17·CV₁. Measured (4×10⁶ draws): 0.516 / 0.532 / 0.565 / 0.662 / 0.826 at CV₁ = 0.005 / 0.01 / 0.02 / 0.05 / 0.10, against a predicted 0.516 / 0.532 / 0.563 / 0.659 / 0.817 — and 0.500 for both shortcut and Fieller at every CV₁. The asymmetry GROWS as α shrinks (coefficient 4.49·√w₁ at α=0.05, 9.59 at 0.01, 19.24 at 0.001), so it is worst in the corrected two-tier tier. Requirement: the A/A matrix must record the sign of each false positive, not just the count.

Coverage as a function of (injected effect size × CV₁) separates all three cleanly, because their coverage surfaces are ORTHOGONAL. Shortcut: coverage depends on θ and w₁ only — 0.951/0.939/0.905 at θ = 0/+0.10/+0.50, the same at CV₁ = 0.02 and at 0.45, and OVER-covers for negative θ (0.970 at −0.20). Delta: depends on CV₁ only — 0.951/0.952/0.952/0.949/0.939/0.930 at CV₁ = 0.02/0.05/0.10/0.20/0.30/0.45, flat in θ. Fieller: 0.950 everywhere. A 2-D sweep over injected relative effects {−50%, −20%, 0, +10%, +20%, +50%} × denominator CV {0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30} identifies which formula is implemented without reading any source.

Power under an injected effect, IF the reject flag is derived from the relative CI rather than from the absolute p-value: the shortcut's power curve is asymmetric in the sign of the injected effect (over-rejects at +20%, under-rejects at −20%, by roughly the factor 1 ± θw₁), whereas Fieller's is symmetric in the sense that it exactly tracks the absolute test at every injected effect. If the engine derives reject from the p-value instead, this prediction is null — and that null result itself confirms the coupling.

Unbounded-branch rate is a direct, countable signature. Inject a low-CV₁ regime (a rare conversion, or a metric near zero) so that CV₁ ≈ 0.30: Fieller must decline to produce a bounded relative interval in ≈ 8.5% of A/A splits (39.7% at CV₁ = 0.45, 0.12% at 0.20, 0% at ≤ 0.10), while shortcut and delta return a finite interval 100% of the time. Over the same splits Fieller's coverage stays 0.950 and delta's falls to 0.939 (0.930 at CV₁ = 0.45). An implementation that never emits 'unbounded' is not Fieller regardless of what its formula looks like.

Ratio-metric variance errors are unmistakable in A/A FPR because they are multiplicative on the SE at ALL parameter values, including the null: omitting the within-unit cross-moment gives FPR ≈ 0.019 (SE ×1.20) or 0.010 (×1.31) against nominal 0.05; computing the variance at the impression level gives FPR ≈ 0.123 at a design effect of 1.61. Contrast this with the between-arms case where the analogous-sounding omission is invisible at the null — an A/A matrix is the right instrument for the ratio-metric covariance and the wrong instrument for the arm-means one.

Point-estimate bias is measurable in the A/A matrix as a nonzero mean of θ̂ across placebo splits: predicted E[θ̂] = (1+θ)·CV₁², i.e. +0.0025 at CV₁ = 0.05 and +0.010 at CV₁ = 0.10, systematically POSITIVE and identical for every interval method (it is a property of the estimator, not the interval). If the A/A matrix already records the mean placebo effect, this is a free calibration check on CV₁ itself — and a nonzero mean placebo effect should NOT be read as a broken randomization until this term is subtracted.
open_questions: Whether the engine's reject flag is derived from the relative CI or from the absolute p-value. If from the CI, switching to Fieller changes no decision (proved) but switching to delta/Wald changes decisions near the boundary and introduces the sign asymmetry; if from the p-value, the CI choice affects only reported widths and the discriminating power/FPR predictions above collapse to coverage-only.

How to render a non-symmetric interval in a UI and a BI schema that presumably assume effect ± half-width. Options: store (lo, hi) directly and expose SE separately as a power/MDE input with a documented note that hi − lo ≠ 2·z·SE; or store (lo, hi, se). This is an interface decision, not a statistical one, but it will decide whether Fieller is adoptable.

Whether Fieller's exactness survives the plug-in of V̂₁, V̂₂ from heavy-tailed data at the engine's smaller cutoffs. Fieller is exact for KNOWN variances under normality; with estimated variances and Welch df it is approximate, and I have not quantified the residual error at, say, n = 10³ with skewness 10. A simulation over the actual metric distributions would settle it and is worth doing before adopting 'exact' as a claim in user-facing docs.

For binary metrics, whether Fieller-with-unconstrained-variance or the true score interval (Miettinen–Nurminen, which uses null-constrained p̃_j) is preferred. They agree to O(1/n) and at n ≥ 10⁴ the difference is irrelevant, but at low event counts MN is better documented. Adopting MN would mean special-casing a metric family, which conflicts with a plugin architecture — that trade is a design decision I cannot make blind.

The interaction of Fieller with a Benjamini–Hochberg read-time correction. BH selects an effective α per comparison AFTER the intervals are computed; since Fieller's shape depends on α through g, the interval must be recomputed at the BH-selected α rather than rescaled. Whether the resulting collection of intervals still has the intended FDR-adjusted joint interpretation is a question I have not resolved (it is the standard 'BH-adjusted confidence intervals' problem, which is known to be subtle, and the nonlinearity in α may make it worse).

Whether to bias-correct the point estimate by CV̂₁². It is the right thing for portfolio-level aggregation and the wrong thing for reproducibility against a hand-computed m̂₂/m̂₁ − 1. I lean toward reporting the uncorrected ratio and exposing the correction as a diagnostic, but that is a product judgment.

For metrics that can be negative, whether a symmetric normalized measure Δ/((m̂₁+m̂₂)/2) should be offered as a distinct estimand or whether the relative effect should simply be suppressed. Offering it risks users reading it as a percent change, which it is not.
sources: Fieller, E. C. (1954). 'Some Problems in Interval Estimation.' JRSS-B 16(2):175–185. (Also Fieller 1940, JRSS Suppl. 7:1–64.) The original test-inversion construction for a ratio of normal means.

Gleser, L. J. & Hwang, J. T. (1987). 'The Nonexistence of 100(1−α)% Confidence Sets of Finite Expected Diameter in Errors-in-Variables and Related Models.' Annals of Statistics 15(4):1351–1362. The impossibility theorem: any valid CI for a ratio must be unbounded with positive probability — this is why delta/log intervals cannot have uniform coverage.
Cochran, W. G. (1977). Sampling Techniques, 3rd ed., Ch. 6. Ratio estimators: the bias ≈ CV² result and the classical 'denominator CV < 0.1' rule of thumb; also the n > 25γ² skewness rule (Ch. 2).

Cramér, H. (1946). Mathematical Methods of Statistics, §27.7. The delta method as an asymptotic statement about the limiting distribution rather than about literal moments (which for a ratio need not exist).

Katz, D., Baptista, J., Azen, S. P. & Pike, M. C. (1978). 'Obtaining Confidence Intervals for the Risk Ratio in Cohort Studies.' Biometrics 34:469–474. The log-scale relative-risk interval, Var(log RR) = (1−p₁)/(n₁p₁) + (1−p₂)/(n₂p₂).

Koopman, P. A. R. (1984). 'Confidence Intervals for the Ratio of Two Binomial Proportions.' Biometrics 40:513–517; and Miettinen, O. & Nurminen, M. (1985). 'Comparative Analysis of Two Rates.' Statistics in Medicine 4:213–226. The score intervals for a ratio of proportions — the binary-metric analogue of Fieller with null-constrained variance.

Hinkley, D. V. (1969). 'On the Ratio of Two Correlated Normal Random Variables.' Biometrika 56:635–639; Marsaglia, G. (1965, and 2006 JSS). The exact ratio-of-normals density — the formal basis for 'the ratio has no moments when the denominator straddles zero'.

Deng, A., Knoblich, U. & Lu, J. (2018). 'Applying the Delta Method in Metric Analytics: A Practical Guide with Novel Ideas.' KDD 2018 (arXiv:1803.06336). The canonical industrial treatment of ratio metrics with the randomization unit ≠ analysis unit, i.e. the Var(N − rD)/(n μ_D²) linearization and the design-effect trap.

Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments, Ch. 18 ('Variance Estimation and Improved Sensitivity'). Ratio metrics, the delta method, and the percent-change reporting convention in an A/B setting.

Vaeth, M. (1985). 'On the Use of Wald's Test in Exponential Families.' International Statistical Review 53:199–214; Dagenais, M. G. & Dufour, J.-M. (1991). 'Invariance, Nonlinear Models, and Asymptotic Tests.' Econometrica 59:1601–1615. Wald tests are not invariant to reparameterization — the formal statement of why the delta/Wald relative interval disagrees with the absolute test about the same hypothesis.

Franz, V. H. (2007). 'Ratios: A Short Guide to Confidence Limits and Proper Use.' arXiv:0710.2024. A readable comparison of delta, log and Fieller intervals with simulation evidence broadly matching the coverage tables reproduced here.

Howard, S. R., Ramdas, A., McAuliffe, J. & Sekhon, J. (2021). 'Time-Uniform, Nonasymptotic, Nonparametric Confidence Sequences.' Annals of Statistics 49(2):1055–1080. Relevant only for the note that Fieller is a test inversion and therefore composes with an anytime-valid critical radius in place of z.
